tasks.instruction: Write a discussion response. An effective response contains at least 100 words.

professor.name: Doctor Achebe
professor.text: Having students work together in small groups on learning activities is a popular alternative to teaching the whole class as one large group. The average age of students in a classroom can, of course, be an important consideration when choosing any teaching approach. I'd like us to consider two age groups: very young students (ages 5-11) and older students (ages 14-18). Which age group do you think would benefit more from working in small groups on learning activities? Why?

posts.name: Claire
posts.text: I think young elementary school kids would benefit more from small group activities than high schoolers. Young kids are often more eager to participate and cooperate, whereas teens can be disengaged and distracted during class. Grouping kids when they're young can teach them social skills and get them excited about learning together. High schoolers may prefer independent work where they can focus without distractions from peers.

posts.name: Andrew
posts.text: I think older high school students would benefit more from small group work. Teens tend to be more competitive and motivated to stand out, so working in groups can encourage them to challenge each other intellectually. From my experience in group projects, we pushed each other to think deeper and produce better work than we could have individually.

tasks.sample: In my opinion, older students (ages 14-18) would benefit more from working in small groups on learning activities. One reason is that high school students are at a stage where intellectual development and social interaction play key roles in their learning. In small groups, teens can challenge each other, exchange ideas, and learn from different perspectives, which often leads to deeper understanding and higher-quality work. This fundamentally benefits their ability to tackle more challenging schoolwork in middle and high school. Additionally, older students are typically more self-aware and motivated to perform well in group settings. The competitive nature of high school students can foster a productive environment where they push each other to excel. In contrast, younger students may not yet have the maturity or focus required for effective collaboration. They may get distracted more easily, and their eagerness to participate could be influenced by a need for teacher guidance or one-on-one attention. Therefore, small group activities are more beneficial for older students, as they provide opportunities for intellectual growth, skill development, and peer-driven motivation.
